L830@P14: 5 Conclusion and Outlook
L831@P14: The introduced notion of d-counterfactual cause for a distance function d in transition systems turned
L832@P14: out to be checkable in polynomial time for the distance functions dpref , dHamm, and dLev and it, hence, has
L833@P14: the potential to be employed in efficient tools to provide understandable explanations of the behavior of
L834@P14: a system. In our results for safety effects Φ, one caveat remains: we only considered finite executions
L835@P14: reaching a cause candidate C and satisfying Φ in the input to the checking algorithms. Allowing also
L836@P14: finitely representable, e.g., ultimately periodic paths, constitutes a natural possible extension, which
L837@P14: requires adjustments in the provided algorithms.
L838@P14: The problem of finding good causes remains as future work: Whenever causality can be checked in
L839@P14: polynomial time, there is an obvious non-deterministic polynomial-time upper bound on the problem to
L840@P14: decide whether there are causes below a given size, but the precise complexities are unclear. A further
L841@P14: idea is to use the distance function to assess how good a cause is by considering the distance from the
L842@P14-15: actual execution to the closest executions avoiding a cause. For reachability effects and the prefix and16 Counterfactual Causality for Reachability and Safety
L843@P15: Hamming distance, the set of direct predecessors optimizes this distance. For other distance functions or
L844@P15: safety causes, this measure could, nevertheless, be more useful. The search for similar measures for the
L845@P15: quality of causes constitutes an interesting direction for future work.
L846@P15: In reachability games, we saw that the analogous definition of D-counterfactual causes can be checked
L847@P15: in polynomial time for the Hausdorff-lifting d

L851@P15: of the conceptually simpler D-minimal explanations provides insights into the complications one might

L1020@P19: When checking whether C is a dHamm-counterfactual cause, we have to look at paths not reaching C.
L1021@P19: Hence, we remove all states in C from T to obtain the weighted transition system TC. The question
L1022@P19: is whether, among the path of TC that are most similar to the original execution π according to dHamm,
L1023@P19: there is a path that reaches E. This question is now easy to answer: We compute the shortest path from
L1024@P19: sinit to the last layer k in TC and denote the weight by Wk. If there is no path to layer k anymore, then
L1025@P19: C is unavoidable in T and not a cause. Afterwards, we compute the shortest path from sinit to E in TC
L1026@P19: and call the weight WE. If such a path does not exist, but a path to the kth layer exists, then C is a cause
L1027@P19: because all executions avoiding C also avoid E. Otherwise, we compare the two weights: If WE = Wk,
L1028@P19: then C is not a cause. A shortest path to E in TC is at least as similar to π as any other path in TC
L1029@P19: reaching the last layer. If WE > Wk, then the shortest paths in TC reaching the last layer are the paths in
L1030@P19: T that are most similar to π among all paths avoiding C and none of these paths reaches E. So, in this
L1031@P19: case C is a dHamm-counterfactual cause for E on π.
L1032@P19: As shortest paths in a weighted transition system can be computed in polynomial time and the transformations made to obtain TC are also easily doable in polynomial time, the described procedure can
L1033@P19: solve the problem in polynomial time.
